notes.text: White's pawn takes space in the center, which is White's most common first move.
notes.original: White's most common opening move is to simply try and take control of the center with the move e4.

notes.text: The Sicilian: your c-pawn fights for the d4 square, and many variations follow.
notes.original: This black's most common response and this is the one of the most played openings ever. This is known as the Sicilian Defense. The point of this move is to try and control the crucial d4 square. From this point, the game can be split into so many different variations. I will try to cover as many as possible in separate chapters.

notes.text: White intends d4 to open the position, usually reaching the Open Sicilian.
notes.original: This move will often lead to the Open Sicilian. White intends on playing d4 in order to open up the position. I will show you how to reach the open position.

notes.text: This is the Closed Sicilian, where White avoids d4; your one solid reply is Nc6.
notes.original: This is known as the Closed Sicilian. This is known as the Closed Sicilian because white doesn't intend to play d4 which will open up the position. Black basically has one solid move in this position and that's Nc6.

notes.text: This is an off-beat try against the Sicilian; it is rare, so you needn't study it deeply.
notes.original: Now I'm going to show you some off-beat openings in the Sicilian. You don't necessarily need to know these openings, but as someone that rolls my eyes every time I see this, I want to know how to beat this and maybe you do as well. If you ever see this opening, you can safely assume that white has no idea how to play against the Sicilian. Also note that I'm not going to go into too many different variations because this is not a widely accepted opening.

notes.text: This is Black's most common move, and it leads to many variations after the pawn exchange.
notes.original: This is black's most common move. This can lead into many different variations after the pawn exchange occurs.

notes.text: Developing the knight instead of playing d6 is also possible; this is the Old Sicilian.
notes.original: Black can also play this move. This is known as the Old Sicilian.

notes.text: White's d-pawn now hits your c5 pawn, continuing the plan to open the center.
notes.original: White continues with their plan of opening up the center.

notes.text: You simply trade your c-pawn for White's central pawn.
notes.original: Black should simply exchange their pawn with white's central pawn.

notes.text: This is the Open Sicilian; most variations from here get their own chapter.
notes.original: We have now reached the Open Sicilian. From here many different variations can be played, most of which will be covered in a separate chapter.

notes.text: White again hits your c5 pawn, continuing the plan to open the center.
notes.original: White continues with their plan to open up the center.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your c6 knight; White plans to trade it, then close the position with d3.
notes.original: This will be the first chapter of the Sicilian Defense that I will show from white's perspective. This is because this more of an opening for white and white is the one that chooses to go into this opening. This opening is a very good weapon to use against the Sicilian if white doesn't want to play the open Sicilian and go into main line theory. The idea for white is to give up the bishop for the knight on c6 and then close down the pawn structure with d3. I will go over 4 main responses for black.

notes.text: Simply take the pawn on d4.
notes.original: Black should simply take.

notes.text: Once again you have reached the Open Sicilian position.
notes.original: Once again, we've reached the Open Sicilian position.

notes.text: The Najdorf's a6 stops White's pieces from ever using b5 and prepares your own b5 and a bishop on b7.
notes.original: The Najdorf is one of the sharpest openings in all of chess. This opening was named after Miguel Najdorf who utilized this opening to great success. What the move a6 does is that it prevents any of white's pieces from ever coming to b5. Another thing that this move does is that it prepares for b5 that could be played later on in the game and black could plant their bishop on b7 if they choose to do so. White has quite literally tried everything under the sun against the Najdorf so I will go over as many variations that I can in all separate chapters.

notes.text: Your a6 stops White pieces landing on b5 and prepares b5 with a bishop on b7.
notes.original: The Najdorf is one of the sharpest openings in all of chess. This opening was named after Miguel Najdorf who utilized this opening to great success. What the move a6 does is that it prevents any of white's pieces from ever coming to b5. Another thing that this move does is that it prepares for b5 that could be played later on in the game and black could plant their bishop on b7 if they choose to do so. White has quite literally tried everything under the sun against the Najdorf so I will go over as many variations that I can in this chapter.

notes.text: The English Attack is the most played line and forces you to play aggressively.
notes.original: This could arguably be considered to be the main line of the Sicilian Najdorf as it is the most played but, it's best known as the English Attack. This variation forces black to play aggressively. Black has multiple moves but again, I will only be covering one as this move is simply the only move that isn't too passive

notes.text: White develops solidly and keeps the king away from your likely queenside attack.
notes.original: White can play solidly and just go for quick development instead of trying to be aggressive. This is the third most popular variation and it makes a lot of sense. White also understands that in most lines, black will attack on the queen-side, so it may be better for white to have their king away from all of that action.

notes.text: White backs up the e4 pawn with f3, building a pawn chain.
notes.original: This is a sideline in the Sicilian Najdorf. White simply reinforces the pawn on e4 and creates a pawn chain.

notes.text: This is the main line of the Najdorf, though the English Attack is played more often.
notes.original: This is considered to be the main line of the Najdorf Sicilian although the English Attack is play more commonly than the main line.

notes.text: The Fischer-Sozin Attack fell out of favour once players found the bishop is badly placed on c4.
notes.original: This is the fifth most common variation in the Najdorf which is known as the Lipinitsky or the Fischer-Sozin Attack. It has dropped in popularity because it was discovered that the bishop was not optimally placed on c4.

notes.text: Your e5 is the best move: it hits the knight and forces it back to b3.
notes.original: The best move in this position is to play e5, forcing the knight back to b3. Black can choose to play e6 but it's more passive than e5. e6 is still a viable option for black however where black opts for positional play.

notes.text: This Anti-English move stops White's English Attack by hitting the bishop; the game may transpose.
notes.original: I will cover this variation however because it is a possibility. This is known as the Anti-English. Simply put, black is trying to prevent white from playing the English Attack and this can transpose into a different variation instead or white can try to continue with their plans.

notes.text: You can play e6 here, but it is a bit passive against the English Attack.
notes.original: Black can also play e6 in this position instead of e5. The only problem with this move is that it is slightly too passive and against the English Attack, black's best chances are to play super aggressively.

notes.text: Theory prefers the knight on b3 over f3, even though many engines choose f3.
notes.original: White retreats the knight to b3. White could put the knight back on f3 and a lot of engines will do this, but according to theory, the knight is better on b3 than it is on f3.

notes.text: A natural developing move for you.
notes.original: Natural developing move for black.

notes.text: White prepares a pawn storm; this f3 is typical of the Yugoslav Attack.
notes.original: White prepares the pawn storm with f3. We see this move in the Yugoslav Attack in the Dragon Sicilian.

notes.text: Another developing move, getting ready for you to castle soon.
notes.original: Another developing move for black, preparing to castle shortly.

notes.text: Play the bishop to e7 to prepare castling short.
notes.original: Now black should play Be7, preparing to castle short.

notes.text: White develops the queen and prepares to castle queenside.
notes.original: White is developing as well and is preparing to castle queen-side.

notes.text: White develops the queen, then castles long.
notes.original: Now white will develop the queen and long castle afterwards.

notes.text: You castle, tucking your king away.
notes.original: Black castles.

notes.text: Castle short to tuck your king away.
notes.original: Black should castle.

notes.text: White castles queenside too, and is ready to start an attack.
notes.original: So does white and now white is ready to start an attack.

notes.text: White castles long, transposing into the English Attack main line, where the study stops.
notes.original: White should castle as well. We have transposed into the English Attack which is the main line. I will stop here. Also note that typically, if white played f3, it is unlikely they will want to play the English Attack because if they wanted to, they should've in the first place.

notes.text: You finish developing and are ready to attack too; both sides must know this sharp line.
notes.original: Black finishes their development and is ready for an attack of their own. This is where the position gets really interesting and potentially dangerous. I'd say that this is a line that both sides must know.

notes.text: White starts the attack, threatening g5 to hit your knight, and will bring more pawns forward.
notes.original: White starts the attack with g4, the threat being g5 and white will later bring the rest of the pawns in the attack.

notes.text: You start your own attack with b5, threatening b4, and will bring the a-pawn in later.
notes.original: Black starts their attack also with b5, the threat being b4 and will later bring the a-pawn into the attack as well.

notes.text: White's pawn on g5 attacks your knight on f6 and threatens to take it.
notes.original: White continues their attack and threatens to capture the knight on f6.

notes.text: You needn't move the knight: b4 attacks White's knight on c3 instead.
notes.original: Black actually does not have to move the knight and instead they could play b4, threatening to capture white's knight on c3.

notes.text: Theory and engines prefer moving your knight away rather than taking on f6, though that is still playable.
notes.original: Both theory and the engines agree that it is best to move the knight out of the way rather than to take on f6. The reason is because the queen is on the same diagonal as the c3 knight and if both sides were to capture each other's knights, white would be forced to capture the pawn. However, gxf6 is still a viable option.

notes.text: Taking on f6 isn't bad, but it isn't White's best; retreating the knight is better.
notes.original: White COULD take on f6 and a lot of amateurs playing against the Najdorf probably will take if they're unsure about what they're doing. This is by no means a bad move but it's not the best move for white. Instead white should just retreat the knight.

notes.text: Your knight steps aside and adds protection to the d6 pawn, but the tension remains.
notes.original: Black should move their knight out of the way as well, over defending the d6 pawn . The tension is anything but gone however..

notes.text: White's f4 hits your e5 pawn; the engine takes it, but this line offers you more chances.
notes.original: White now continues their attack with f4. The engine suggests to take the pawn but instead I will show you a more interesting line which in my opinion, leads to more chances with black and white is likely to blunder..

notes.text: Keep attacking with a5; the obvious threat is a4.
notes.original: Black should continue with their attack, the obvious threat being a4.

notes.text: White's pawn on f5 attacks your bishop on e6 and threatens to capture it.
notes.original: White continues the pawn march and is threatening to capture the bishop on e6.

notes.text: You needn't move the bishop: a4 attacks White's knight on b3 instead.
notes.original: Black again doesn't have to move their piece and instead, they can play a4 which is threatening to capture the knight. Black can take the knight with the bishop but I do not suggest it so I will not show the line.

notes.text: White leaves this knight for you to take; this tricky sacrifice is more common than simply taking your bishop.
notes.original: White can take the bishop immediately or they can give up the knight in this fashion which is more commonly played by white. This move is very hard to see over the board and is not expected to be played by someone who doesn't know their theory.

notes.text: Taking on e6 is better for you: White may blunder, and your rook gets the f-file.
notes.original: White COULD take on e6 here but this is honestly better for black as it leads to more of a chance of white blundering and it now opens up the f-file for the rook.

notes.text: Take the knight; the moves that follow are forced.
notes.original: Black should capture the knight, this is not a free piece because the bishop on e6 is trapped. The following moves are now forced.

notes.text: White must retake with the knight; any other capture is a blunder.
notes.original: White MUST capture with the knight only. ANY other move is a blunder. I will show you what happens if white captures incorrectly.

notes.text: Keep the pawn storm going; any other move would be inaccurate and give White an edge.
notes.original: Black must continue their pawn storm in order to keep their chances alive. Any other move would be inaccurate and white would gain an advantage.

notes.text: White has to play this king move, or you gain an advantage.
notes.original: White must play this move or else black will gain an advantage.

notes.text: Capturing on c2 with check is your only move.
notes.original: Another only move in this position, black must capture the c-pawn with check.

notes.text: White must recapture with the knight, or you gain an advantage again.
notes.original: White MUST capture with the knight or else black will once again gain an advantage.

notes.text: This is the best way for you to give up the bishop.
notes.original: This is the best way for black to give up the bishop.

notes.text: White simply recaptures your bishop on b3 with the a-pawn.
notes.original: White should know recapture the bishop.

notes.text: You take the pawn: your pawn now attacks the knight on c2 and opens the a-file for your rook.
notes.original: Black should take the pawn, threatening to capture the knight and opening up the rook.

notes.text: Na3 is White's only move; anything else loses completely or even allows checkmate.
notes.original: Another only move, any other move will be completely losing and/or blunder checkmate. I will go ahead and show you the most likely blunders if white does not play this move.

notes.text: Your knight escapes the cramped position and lands on a strong central square.
notes.original: Now black tries to uncramp their pieces and centralizes their knight.

notes.text: White keeps the pawn storm going with h4, so you must be very careful.
notes.original: White continues the pawn storm with h4. Black needs to be very very careful here.

notes.text: Attack White's weakness: your rook swings to a4 and hits the e4 pawn.
notes.original: At this point, black needs to attack white's weaknesses. White's main weakness is the e-pawn.

notes.text: White's bishop steps between your rook and the e4 pawn, indirectly protecting it.
notes.original: White indirectly defends e4 by blocking the rook.

notes.text: White's rook on h3 lines up on your loose b3 pawn behind its bishop.
notes.original: White could also play Rh3 here. I believe this move is eyeing down the loose b-pawn.

notes.text: Your queen now eyes the weak e4 pawn along the long diagonal.
notes.original: The queen and rook are now on the same file and the queen is also eyeing down the weak e-pawn.

notes.text: Qe3 is White's best way to guard the e4 pawn, and it stays close to the kingside attack.
notes.original: The best way for white to defend this pawn is with Qe3. The queen is also not very far away from the attack on the king-side.

notes.text: A peculiar move, but it just gives your king a bit more safety before White's coming pawn break.
notes.original: This is a peculiar move but all this move is doing is providing a little bit more safety for the king when white makes the inevitable pawn break.

notes.text: White finally develops the light-squared bishop and attacks your rook at the same time.
notes.original: White finally develops their light-squared bishop and attacks the rook at the same time.

notes.text: Rather than sacrificing the rook, you move it away and attack the bishop on b5.
notes.original: Black can sacrifice the rook for the knight here but it is better to just move the rook out of the attack and attack the bishop. The chess database on lichess ends here but I'm going to go ahead and show you a few more theoretical moves because the position is still not clear and still requires sharp play.

notes.text: Bc3 is the best move according to theory and engines, though not the only one.
notes.original: According to both theory and the engines here, Bc3 is the best move. Not the only move, but the best move.

notes.text: Your rook sacrifice on a3 is brilliant; the engine sees it as dead even, likely a draw.
notes.original: This is a brilliant sacrifice for black. If you notice, the engine gives this position as dead even, meaning that it is most likely to end in a draw with either perfect play or a perpetual check.

notes.text: White's only move is to recapture the rook.
notes.original: Only move for white here is to obviously recapture the rook.

notes.text: Your queen takes the pawn back, and White's exposed king could face mate if White is careless.
notes.original: Queen now recaptures the pawn. The king is very exposed here and checkmate is looming around the corner if white is not careful.

notes.text: Rd2 is White's best move: it just prevents checkmate.
notes.original: Rd2 is the best move in this position. There are other moves but it gives black a slight advantage. All this move does is prevent checkmate.

notes.text: Your knight finally rejoins the game and attacks White's loose bishop on b5.
notes.original: Best move for black is to play Nc7 and finally get their knight back in the game and attacking the loose bishop.

notes.text: White's best move takes the bishop out of danger.
notes.original: Be2 is the best move, getting the bishop out of danger.

notes.text: Rb8 is your only move here; any other move would give White an advantage.
notes.original: Only move for black in this position is to play Rb8. Any other move would give white an advantage.

notes.text: White's bishop move is best because White plans to bring a rook to the c-file.
notes.original: Bd4 is the best move, as white intends to play Rc1 at some point.

notes.text: Your knight heads for the attack and gets ready for White's rook coming to c1.
notes.original: Na6 is best, anticipating Rc1 and trying to get the knight in the attack.

notes.text: White's best move is to capture your knight on e5.
notes.original: The best move is for white to capture the knight.

notes.text: You simply recapture the bishop with your pawn.
notes.original: Black obviously recaptures.

notes.text: White's queen hits your knight, rook and bishop all at once.
notes.original: The following best moves here lead to an interesting line here. The best move is Qa7, attacking both the knight, rook, and bishop.

notes.text: Your bishop leaves its undefended post and attacks White's rook on d2 at the same time.
notes.original: Black moves the only undefended piece and attacks the rook at the same time.

notes.text: White gives back the rook, takes your knight and offers a queen trade.
notes.original: The best move is to actually give the rook back to black and capture the knight, initiating a queen trade.

notes.text: Taking the queen is your only move.
notes.original: Only move for black is to capture the queen.

notes.text: White recaptures your queen with the bishop.
notes.original: White recaptures the queen.

notes.text: You win the free rook and are a pawn up, but the position is still roughly equal.
notes.original: Black now takes the free rook and is up a pawn. The position is still more/less equal.

notes.text: White's bishop goes after your weaknesses, the f7 and b3 pawns.
notes.original: White now attacks black's weaknesses.

notes.text: Your rook attacks the bishop on c4 as it goes after White's weaknesses.
notes.original: Black does the same while also attacking the bishop.

notes.text: White captures the free pawn on f7.
notes.original: White captures the free pawn.

notes.text: You take the free e4 pawn too, and the position is much simpler now.
notes.original: Black also captures the free pawn. I will stop here because I feel that the position has gotten a lot less complicated. I know that this is a lot and trust me, you will probably not get this over the board a ton but, the Najdorf has many heavily analyzed lines and this is one of them. I feel that this is very important for both sides to know them as this is one of the most commonly played openings in chess. Feel free to practice against a computer and to use to engine to find out how to play from this position.

notes.text: White's choice here leads to a clear draw that even intermediate players can convert.
notes.original: Last thing I'll mention is, you probably don't wanna do this as white because it will be a definite draw that even intermediate players can convert.

notes.text: Your rook checks the king and allows a rook exchange.
notes.original: This allows black to exchange rooks.

notes.text: White is forced to trade rooks.
notes.original: White is forced to exchange.

notes.text: Your bishop recaptures the rook, and the game heads for an easy draw.
notes.original: Bishop recaptures the rook. The pawns will soon come off the board and the game should be an easy draw.

notes.text: Don't grab the e-pawn at once; this queen move is the only one that keeps equality.
notes.original: The best move is to not capture the e-pawn straight away and instead play Qa8. This is the only move that keeps the position equal.

notes.text: Qd5 is White's only move here, so expect it.
notes.original: White's only move here is Qd5.

notes.text: Skip the queen trade and sacrifice your rook for the knight; this thematic idea returns in the main line.
notes.original: Black can trade queens here but instead, a much better move is to sacrifice the rook for the knight here. This is a very thematic sacrifice and we see this in the main line as well.

notes.text: White's only move is to recapture on a3.
notes.original: Only move for white is to recapture.

notes.text: Your queen recaptures and threatens mate or a pawn push to promote.
notes.original: Now the queen recaptures, threatening mate and/or promotion.

notes.text: Qd2 is White's best move, one of only two moves in the position.
notes.original: Qd2 is the best move and is one of two of the only moves in the position.

notes.text: Nf6 offers your knight: White gets material, but your bishop will aim down the long diagonal at the king.
notes.original: Here the best move is a rather brilliant move here and that's Nf6. Basically black is saying "go ahead, take my knight". Why is this such a good move? Because although yes, white will be up material-wise, black will have a bishop eyeing down the long-diagonal and joining in on the attack against the king.

notes.text: Bd4 is the most common move. White needn't take the knight, but it is dangerous for unprepared players.
notes.original: The most commonly played move here Bd4. White doesn't have to take the knight and it is probably a little bit too dangerous for white if they don't know what they're doing.

notes.text: Reinforce your e5 knight with Nfd7, so it is protected if White takes it.
notes.original: Black should now play Nfd7, reinforcing the knight if it gets taken.

notes.text: Recapturing the knight is your only move; only two moves have ever been played here.
notes.original: Only move for black is to recapture white's knight. Here two moves have been played ever.

notes.text: Recapturing with the c-pawn is White's best and safest option.
notes.original: cxb3 is white's best and safest option.

notes.text: Recapture the pawn to open the f-file for your rook.
notes.original: Now black should recapture the pawn and open up the f-file for the rook. Here, two moves have ever been played again.

notes.text: Bh3 is the most common move, attacking your weak e6 pawn.
notes.original: The most common being Bh3, attacking black's weakness.

notes.text: Give up this pawn: it can't be defended well, so take the a2 pawn.
notes.original: The best thing for black to do is to give up this pawn as it cannot be defended very well.

notes.text: White's only move is to capture the e6 pawn, with check.
notes.original: Only move for white is to capture the e6 pawn.

notes.text: Moving your king is the only good answer to the check.
notes.original: Only good move for black is to move the king.

notes.text: White prepares to bring the knight into the attack via f5.
notes.original: White now prepares to get their knight in the attack and into f5.

notes.text: Your knight kicks out the bishop on e6.
notes.original: Black should try to kick out the bishop.

notes.text: The bishop should retreat to c4.
Qa8 is your only move that doesn't give White a slight advantage.
notes.original: Qa8 is the only move for black that doesn't give white a slight advantage.

notes.text: White's rook takes over the open f-file and wants to trade rooks.
notes.original: White now challenges black's open file and wants to trade rooks.

notes.text: You should take this rook.
notes.original: Black should indeed take this rook.

notes.text: White's only move is to recapture the rook.
Now you should check the king with your rook.
notes.original: Now black should check the king.

notes.text: White has only one legal move here.
notes.original: Only legal move for white.

notes.text: Now you capture the rook.
notes.original: Black now captures the rook.

notes.text: White must recapture with the bishop; any other move gives you an edge.
notes.original: The only move for white here is to capture with the bishop. Any other move will give black an edge.

notes.text: Strike with d5. The theory ends here, and both sides are doing fine.
notes.original: Now black should strike with d5. I will end the theory here but both sides are doing fine here. I do believe however that there are better and easier lines to play that don't include taking the bishop all the way back on move 16.

notes.text: Take the knight: your pawn lands on c3 with an attack on White's queen.
notes.original: Black should capture white's knight now. Now we see the problem with not retreating the knight, it allows black to take the knight with an attack on the queen.

notes.text: White has to take back with the queen.
notes.original: White's only move is to take back with the queen.

notes.text: Retake with the knight: taking with the bishop loses the d-pawn, and taking with the g-pawn weakens your king.
notes.original: Black's only move is to take back with the knight. This is because if you take the bishop, you lose the d-pawn and if you take with the g-pawn, you weaken your king drastically.

notes.text: White's knight on a5 stops your a-pawn from advancing for now.
notes.original: Now white should play Na5, stopping black from pushing the a-pawn temporarily. From here the game branches out to multiple different lines and black is doing okay here.

notes.text: White can retreat the bishop, and the game may transpose to another line.
notes.original: White can retreat the bishop and again, this can transpose to a different line.

notes.text: White's alternative is to bring the bishop to g3 instead of c1.
notes.original: This is an alternative to putting the bishop back on c1. Rather, White can try to put their bishop on g3 instead.

notes.text: Your knight goes back to f6, and White can try the English Attack again or another line.
notes.original: Black puts their knight back on f6. White can either try to play the English again or they may try to play a different variation of the Najdorf.

notes.text: Your pawn threatens White's bishop.
notes.original: Black is threatening the bishop.

notes.text: White shouldn't retreat to c1, or the bishop's earlier moves would be wasted time.
notes.original: White shouldn't retreat to c1 or they would have just wasted their time.

notes.text: Your pawn threatens the bishop once more.
notes.original: Threatening the bishop once more.

notes.text: White puts the bishop on g3, safe from your pawn advance.
notes.original: White plants their bishop on g3.

notes.text: Your bishop takes the long diagonal, but the study thinks this line wastes time; English Attack lines suit you better.
notes.original: Black puts their bishop on the long diagonal and from this point forward, the game branches out. In my opinion, this variation is a waste of time and black is better off playing one of the English Attack main lines.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn challenges the knight on d4 and punishes White's passive f3.
notes.original: Black can play e6 but I'm only gonna cover e5 because e6 somewhat justifies the move f3 as it is too passive. So the move e5 tries to punish white for not playing more aggressively and challenges the knight in the center.

notes.text: The knight retreats to b3, really its only good square.
notes.original: This is really the only good square for white's knight to go to.

notes.text: Develop your light-squared bishop to e6.
notes.original: Now black should Be6, developing the light-squared bishop.

notes.text: White develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares to castle long.
notes.original: White will develop their dark-squared bishop and prepare to castle long.

notes.text: After castling you have already equalized, so White gains little from this f3 line.
notes.original: This is another line that can be played if white plays f3. Black has already equalized however so I don't see why white would want to play this.

notes.text: Be2 is passive, so answer aggressively with e5, hitting the knight on d4.
notes.original: Because Be2 is a passive move from white, black should play aggressively with e5.

notes.text: White retreats the knight to b3, the best square for it.
notes.original: White should retreat the knight to b3. This is the best square for the knight.

notes.text: Develop the bishop to e7 and prepare to castle.
notes.original: Black should now develop and prepare to castle.

notes.text: White uses the moment to castle short.
notes.original: White should take this time to castle.

notes.text: You castle short as well.
notes.original: So should black.

notes.text: White keeps developing with the bishop to e3.
notes.original: Now white continues to develop their other pieces.

notes.text: You develop your bishop too, matching White's development.
notes.original: So does black.

notes.text: White brings the queen to d2, which connects the rooks.
notes.original: White now develops the queen, connecting the rooks.

notes.text: With this knight out, you are nearly finished developing.
notes.original: Black is nearly finished with their development.

notes.text: Play e6 here; pushing the pawn to e5 instead would be a mistake.
notes.original: Black should continue with e6 here. e5 would be a mistake in this position

notes.text: White's most common move is f4, preparing an attack; you have two main replies, one far more common.
notes.original: White's most common move is f4, preparing to launch an attack against black. From here black has two main responses with one being played much more commonly than the other.

notes.text: Your queen is the main move: it eyes the b2 pawn and the knight on d4.
notes.original: Qb6 is the main move and is the also the top engine choice in this position. Black prevents white from playing the usual Qf3 and is eyeing down the b-pawn a.k.a. the poison pawn and the knight on d4.

notes.text: Be7 is probably your safest choice: it avoids the poisoned pawn and goes for development.
notes.original: Be7 is another way that black can approach this position and is probably the safest way for black to play. This move avoids the poisoned pawn variation and black goes for development instead.

notes.text: White usually lets you take the poison pawn; Qd2 avoids a fork of your rook and knight.
notes.original: White will usually let black take the poison pawn and change their plans, castling short instead. Qd2 is an important move because it always black to take the pawn without forking the rook and the knight on c3 (If white had played Qf3 for example..)

notes.text: Just take the b2 pawn; it is a free pawn.
notes.original: Black should just take this pawn as it is just a free pawn.

notes.text: White's rook now uses the open b-file against you, which is why the pawn was given up.
notes.original: White will now use the open b-file against black which is why they allowed for black to take the b-pawn.

notes.text: Qa3 is your only move, getting the queen to safety; White has two ideas here.
notes.original: Qa3 is the only move for black, getting the queen to safety. There are two moves that white can play here and I will go over both.

notes.text: White's pawn hits your d6 pawn and your knight; you have two almost equally common replies.
notes.original: e5 is the main move and has been played more than the engine recommendation, f5. White just attacks black's center with the e-pawn rather than the f-pawn and it also attacks black's knight. There are two ways black can play this and they are almost played evenly.

notes.text: The engine prefers f5, which is playable, but e5 leads to more forcing lines.
notes.original: The engine recommends f5 rather than e5 in this position. f5 is viable option for white but I think that e5 leads to more forcing lines.

notes.text: Taking on e5 is the most common reply, rather than h6.
notes.original: dxe5 is the most common move in this position rather than creating an equal threat with h6.

notes.text: This sideline uses your h-pawn to try to kick out White's bishop.
notes.original: h6 is the sideline, attempting to kick out white's bishop.

notes.text: White recaptures with the pawn, which still attacks your knight.
notes.original: White will obviously recapture with the pawn, still attacking the knight

notes.text: Get your knight out of danger; now White's e5 pawn is under some pressure.
notes.original: Black should get their knight out of danger, note that the e-pawn is now under some pressure.

notes.text: Ne4 is the most common move here; note that the e5 pawn cannot be taken.
notes.original: Ne4 is the most common move in this position. Note that the pawn on e5 CANNOT be taken.

notes.text: Your h-pawn attacks the bishop on g5; this is the main move.
notes.original: h6 is the main move in this position, obviously threatening the bishop.

notes.text: Taking the e5 pawn now loses: White wins after Nb5.
notes.original: If black takes the pawn then white is winning after Nb5.

notes.text: White retreats the bishop but keeps it on the same diagonal.
notes.original: The bishop should retreat but stay on the same diagonal.

notes.text: Now take the other loose pawn, on a2.
notes.original: Black should take the other loose pawn on a2 now.

notes.text: White gets the rook out of danger and centralizes it on the d-file.
notes.original: White gets their rook out of danger and centralizes it as well.

notes.text: Your queen forks the knight on e4 and the e5 pawn.
notes.original: The best move for black is Qd5, forking the knight and the e-pawn.

notes.text: White's queen steps to e3 to protect the knight on e4.
notes.original: The best move is Qe3, protecting the knight.

notes.text: You are three pawns up, but your pieces are undeveloped, so the position is equal; stay sharp.
notes.original: Now black is THREE pawns up and yet the position is still 0.0. Why? Black has almost zero development but in exchange, they have three pawns. Note that both sides need to stay very sharp from here on out and you will see a bunch of only moves from both sides.

notes.text: White's bishop to e2 is the only move that keeps equality, and it prepares castling.
notes.original: This is the only move here that keeps the position equal, preparing to castle.

notes.text: Bf2 is a blunder White sometimes plays; it loses to your knight move Nc5 or Nf6.
notes.original: I will go ahead and show you one blunder that I've seen which is Bf2. This is losing because of Nf6/Nc5. I will show you the line briefly.

notes.text: Your bishop pins the d4 knight to White's queen; another only move.
notes.original: Another only move in the position is Bc5, pinning the knight to the queen.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your queen; here only two moves are good.
notes.original: Another only move, attacking the queen. Here there are only two good moves.

notes.text: Taking on d4 is the most common move; White must keep queens on or be worse.
notes.original: The most common move is Bxd4. Again, white needs to keep their queen on the board or they will be losing.

notes.text: White's rook retakes on d4; it is the only move.
notes.original: Rxd4 is the only move in the position.

notes.text: Your queen checks the king and escapes with a gain of time; another only move.
notes.original: And ANOTHER only move is Qa5+, gaining a tempo on the king and allowing the queen to escape.

notes.text: White blocks the check with the rook on d2; another only move.
notes.original: You guessed it, ANOTHER only move is Rd2, interposing the check.

notes.text: Castling is once more your only move.
notes.original: Castling is the only move once more.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your rook on f8; another only move, though you have several replies.
notes.original: Bd6 is ANOTHER only move, attacking the rook. There are quite a few options that black can play here.

notes.text: Moving the rook to d8 is by far the most common way to save it.
notes.original: By far the most common move is Rd8, simply getting the rook out of danger.

notes.text: White's queen backs up the d6 bishop and lines up on your king behind the g7 pawn.
notes.original: Qg3 is the main and best move in this position, reinforcing the bishop and x-raying the king. The position has calmed down a bit the array of only moves have pretty much ended, but both sides still need to be be careful because it is very easy for either side to gain an advantage.

notes.text: Developing the knight to c6 uncramps your pieces; it is the main move.
notes.original: Nc6 is the main move here, simply developing the knight and uncramping the pieces.

notes.text: White's bishop to c7 is the only move that doesn't give you a slight edge.
notes.original: Bc7 is the only move here that doesn't give black a slight advantage.

notes.text: Your queen checks the king, gaining a tempo.
notes.original: Qa1+ is the best move, gaining a tempo on the king.

notes.text: White's rook blocks the check and attacks your queen, gaining a tempo.
notes.original: Rd1 is the best move, now gaining a tempo on the queen.

notes.text: Queen to b2 is the only move that doesn't hand White too much of an advantage.
notes.original: Now Qb2 is the only move that doesn't give white too much of an advantage here. There's quite a few moves that white can play in this position.

notes.text: Castling is by far the most common move; White cares little about your rook on d8.
notes.original: The most common move by far is to just castle, as white isn't super interested in this useless rook on d8.

notes.text: Moving the rook to f8 is your only way to avoid tactics from White.
notes.original: Rf8 is the only move here that avoids any kind of tactical play from white.

notes.text: White's bishop hits your rook on f8 again and lands on a more useful square.
notes.original: Now white is attacking black's rook once more and is getting the bishop to a more useful position.

notes.text: If White takes your rook, your knight takes the bishop with check and forks king and queen.
notes.original: A tricky but pretty obvious move from black. If white takes the rook, then black will capture the bishop and fork the king and queen.

notes.text: Bishop to g4 is White's only move that avoids giving you a slight edge.
notes.original: Bg4 is the only move that doesn't give black a slight edge.

notes.text: Your only move: the knight hits White's queen and d6 bishop, forcing White to give up the bishop pair.
notes.original: Only move for black once again, attacking the queen and bishop on d6, forcing white to give up the bishop pair.

notes.text: White has to take your knight on f5.
notes.original: White must take the knight.

notes.text: Retaking with the e-pawn is your only move.
notes.original: Only move for black obviously.

notes.text: White's best move takes the knight out of danger, and White doesn't have to take your rook on f8.
notes.original: Nc3 is the best move here, getting the knight out of danger, again white doesn't have to take the rather bad rook on f8.

notes.text: You can finally get your rook out of danger.
notes.original: Black however can finally get their rook out of danger.

notes.text: The knight on d5 is White's best move and becomes a really powerful piece.
notes.original: Nd5 is the best move in the position, getting a really powerful knight for white.

notes.text: The most common move: your rook lands on the second rank, hitting White's c2 and g2 pawns.
notes.original: Re2 is the most common move in this position and is targeting white's weakness.

notes.text: White's usual check nearly forces you to give up your rook by capturing the knight.
notes.original: White usually plays Ne7 here. This is a tricky move because it somewhat forces black to give up the rook in this position.

notes.text: You should give up the rook by taking the knight.
notes.original: So black should give up the rook.

notes.text: White should obviously take the rook.
Even a rook down, your passed queenside pawns help; the game looks drawish, but stay careful.
notes.original: Now black can capture on c2. Note that although black is playing without a second rook but they can use their passed queen-side pawns as assets. Neither side is in much danger however and the game is likely to end in a draw. But I would say just be extra careful if you're playing as black.

notes.text: White's most challenging move: the bishop prepares to go to c3.
notes.original: White's most challenging move is Bb4, preparing to go to c3.

notes.text: Stepping the king to h7 is the best move here.
notes.original: Kh7 is the best move for sure, stepping out of pins from the queen and the bishop.

notes.text: White's bishop should go to c3.
notes.original: The bishop should go to c3.

notes.text: Pushing the f-pawn is your only move in this position.
notes.original: f6 is the only move in the position.

notes.text: Rd2 is White's best attempt at creating an attack.
notes.original: Rd2 is white's best attempt at creating an attack.

notes.text: Qb3 is your only move; if the bishop moved instead, you could trade queens and be winning.
notes.original: Qb3 is the only move, this is because should the bishop move, black can trade queens and be winning.

notes.text: White should take the f5 pawn with the rook now.
notes.original: White should take this pawn now.

notes.text: Your knight on e5 is the best move; it stops White from finding tactics.
notes.original: Ne5 as the best move, as black wants to prevent any sort of tactical play that can give white an advantage.

notes.text: White's best move is to retreat the rook.
Keep your queen near the action so White has no dangerous tactics; you will mostly be defending.
notes.original: Black needs to keep their queen near the action to help prevent any kind of dangerous tactical play. I'll end here with theory/best moves as I do not believe the position as too complicated from this point forward. You probably don't need to know all of this theory but it goes to show just how sharp the Najdorf can be. Note that black will most likely be defending this position rather than being super aggressive. However, if white slips up then black can use their passed queen-side pawns at any moment to try and gain an advantage. If black can get the queens off the board as well, they will surely be winning. Note that if white captures the knight, you can only take with the f-pawn.

notes.text: With queens off the board you are completely fine, and still three pawns up.
notes.original: Basically, since the queen's are off the board, black is completely okay now. They will develop and note that they are already three pawns up.

notes.text: White's knight attacks your queen, and taking it is very dangerous.
notes.original: Nb5 is obviously attacking the queen. Black cannot take this knight or else it is checkmate.

notes.text: The check on d3 is your best move, though it is hard to find.
notes.original: The best move but a really hard move to find in this position is Nd3+.

notes.text: White should capture your knight with the bishop.
notes.original: White should capture this knight with the bishop.

notes.text: You can take the knight now, though you are still losing.
notes.original: Now black can capture this knight although they are still losing.

notes.text: White's bishop recaptures with check, so your reply has to be chosen carefully.
notes.original: The bishop should recapture here. There are only two moves that don't lead to checkmate.

notes.text: Block the check with your bishop; Bd7 is the best move.
notes.original: The best move is Bd7.

notes.text: White should castle here.
notes.original: White should castle.

notes.text: Your h-pawn tries to kick White's bishop off the g5 square.
notes.original: Black will try to kick out your bishop.

notes.text: White's bishop retreats but stays on the same diagonal.
notes.original: White should retreat but stay on the same diagonal.

notes.text: Throwing in this check with your bishop is your best move.
notes.original: Throwing in this check is black's best move.

notes.text: White's king slides over to h1, out of the check.
notes.original: The king should slide over.

notes.text: Now you should castle.
notes.original: Now black should castle.

notes.text: White's knight checks your king; you shouldn't take it, though you're already losing.
notes.original: White should check the king with the knight. This shouldn't be taken but black is already losing so I will show u what happens anyway.

notes.text: Slide your king over to h8 instead of taking the knight.
notes.original: The king should slide over.

notes.text: Taking the knight with your pawn is even worse for you.
notes.original: If black takes then they are doing even worse.

notes.text: After the exchanges, White has come out a piece ahead.
notes.original: Now white is up a piece after a bunch of exchnages.

notes.text: Black is doing horribly here, so don't take the pawn.
notes.original: I will stop here but as you can see, black is doing horribly so don't take the pawn :)

notes.text: The moral once more: don't take the pawn.
notes.original: The line goes but moral of the story once more... don't take the pawn.

notes.text: White's bishop is stronger than your knight, so White avoids trading it.
notes.original: White's bishop is clearly stronger than black's knight so white should not trade pieces here.

notes.text: You take on e5 so that, after White recaptures, you can play g5.
notes.original: Now black will take the e-pawn, black does this so that white can recapture and allow black to play g5.

notes.text: White recaptures and attacks your knight again.
notes.original: White recaptures and attacks the knight once more.

notes.text: Now your g-pawn can go to g5 and attack the bishop on h4.
notes.original: Now black can play g5 without any fear of it being taken.

notes.text: White's queen comes to f3, preparing to castle long.
notes.original: White will then continue with Qf3, preparing to castle long.

notes.text: Developing your queen to c7 is a common choice here.
notes.original: A common queen developing move for black.

notes.text: White castles long, putting the king on c1.
notes.original: Now white will castle.

notes.text: You keep developing your pieces.
notes.original: Black continues their development.

notes.text: White continues the pawn storm toward your king.
notes.original: White will continue their pawn storm towards the king.

notes.text: Now you start your own pawn march toward White's king.
notes.original: Black will now start their pawn march towards white's king also.

notes.text: White's bishop takes your f6 knight to get rid of it.
notes.original: Here, white gets rid of the f6 knight.

notes.text: Recapture with the knight; it is your only good move here.
notes.original: Recapturing with the knight is black's only good move in the position.

notes.text: White's bishop eyes d5, so keep guarding it with e6 instead of the risky e5.
notes.original: Here black does NOT want to play e5 here because it just too risky. The reason is because the bishop on c4 is already looking at the d5 square and black should keep defending it with e6. This also prepares to develop the bishop to e7 as we usually see in most Najdorf lines. This will transpose into Scheveningen lines.

notes.text: White retreats the bishop to b3 first, since you are going to play b5 anyway.
notes.original: White should play Bb3 rather than castling straight away because they know that black is going to play b5 anyway.

notes.text: Play b5 at once: your pawn covers c4, so White's pieces cannot come back there.
notes.original: Black should play b5 immediately which is the main line of the Fischer-Sozin Attack, preventing the bishop or any other piece from coming back to c4. In some lines, black can go for b4 later on. If white is not careful, black can play b4 and then take the pawn on e4. This variation of the Fischer-Sozin Attack becomes known as the Flank Variation with b5.

notes.text: Nbd7 is playable but less popular, since White gets to attack very early.
notes.original: Another try for black is to play Nbd7 rather than playing b5 straight away. This is playable but it's less popular for a reason and that's because white gets to be super aggressive super early.

notes.text: White castles here, which is the move White should make.
notes.original: Now white should castle here.

notes.text: Develop your bishop and get ready to castle.
notes.original: Black should develop and prepare to castle as well.

notes.text: Pushing b4 is playable, but it is not very common.
notes.original: A lot of players will play b4 in this position and it is playable but it is not very common.

notes.text: White's queen backs up e5, a push that would win quickly if you are careless.
notes.original: White will usually play Qf3 here. Why? If black is not carefully, e5 will instantly win the game.

notes.text: With your queen on c7, you can answer White's sneaky e5 with Bb7 without losing the bishop.
notes.original: Black should play Qc7 here. This is because if white tries to go for the sneaky e5 line, black can now play Bb7 without losing the bishop.

notes.text: Qb6 also stops e5 and hits the loose knight on d4.
notes.original: Black can also play Qb6 with the same idea of preventing e5 and also targeting the loose knight on d4.

notes.text: White's queen on g3 threatens to take your g7 pawn.
notes.original: White should play Qg3, threatening to take the g7 pawn.

notes.text: Castle your king to safety.
notes.original: Black should castle.

notes.text: Bh6 looks scary, but you can easily meet the mate threat on g7 with Ne8 or Nh5.
notes.original: This looks scary but it's really not. If black is stupid than obviously there's a mate threat, but it can easily be taken care of with Nh5 or Ne8.

notes.text: Ne8 is the most common and most natural reply; now both sides keep developing.
notes.original: Ne8 is the most common and more human move may I add. Now both sides continue to develop.

notes.text: White centralizes one of the rooks.
notes.original: White centralizes one of their rooks.

notes.text: Develop the bishop to d7; Bb7 would leave your e-pawn with less support and let White play f4.
notes.original: Black develops their bishop. There's no point in Playing Bb7 because the pawn is well protected and black is going to play Nc6 anyway. White will have an advantage if black chooses to play Bb7 because now there's less reinforcement for the e-pawn and white can justifiably play f4, f5. They can also go for a tactical and much better line in which white sacrifice the light-squared bishop for the pawn, leading to a knight fork of the rook and the queen.

notes.text: Nf3 is the most common way for White to continue after Bd7.
notes.original: This is the most common way to continue after Bd7.

notes.text: White can play aggressively with f4 instead of Nf3.
notes.original: White can choose to be aggressive in this position and play f4 rather than Nf3.

notes.text: Keep developing your pieces.
notes.original: Black should continue their development.

notes.text: White's bishop is more active on f4, and it pins your d6 pawn to your queen.
notes.original: White moves the bishop where it is more active, it is also pinning the pawn to the queen.

notes.text: Step your queen out of the way of the pin.
notes.original: Black should just step out of the way of the pin.

notes.text: White has now centralized both rooks.
Your b-pawn finally kicks the knight off c3.
notes.original: Now black will finally play b4, kicking out white's knight from c3.

notes.text: Ne2 is White's best retreat; the engines also like Na4, but it looks far less human.
notes.original: White's best move is to play Ne2. Na4 is suggested by the engines as well but it seems a lot less human and has never been played before.

notes.text: Your e-pawn attacks White's bishop on f4.
notes.original: Black can take this time to play e5, attacking white's bishop.

notes.text: White's bishop steps out of danger and offers to trade on e7.
notes.original: White offers a trade of bishops and gets out of danger.

notes.text: Rather than trade dark bishops, you aim at White's much more active light bishop.
notes.original: Black can accept this trade but it is more common for black to try and trade off the light-squared bishop instead because white's is so much more active.

notes.text: Nh4 is White's most common move: if your light bishop goes, f5 becomes a target for the knight.
notes.original: The engine doesn't suggest this move but Nh4 is to most common move for white. This is because if black trades off the light-squared bishop, f5 is permanently weak and white will try to plant their knight there. There's a game with Boris Gelfand and Garry Kasparov with this position that you can check out.

notes.text: Now you trade off the dark-squared bishops.
notes.original: Now black should trade off the dark-squared bishop.

notes.text: White has no choice but to recapture.
notes.original: Only move for white is to recapture.

notes.text: Your knight hits the b3 bishop, but White will turn the tables with Bd5.
notes.original: Black can play Na5, attempting to force white to trade off the light-squared bishop but instead, white will force black to make the exchange.

notes.text: White's bishop attacks your queen, with the rook on a8 behind it.
notes.original: Best move for white is to play Bd5, skewering the queen and rook.

notes.text: Just take the bishop; Nc6 would waste a move.
notes.original: Black should just take the bishop. They can play Nc6 but that would just be a wasted move.

notes.text: White recaptures with the rook, which also attacks your knight on a5.
notes.original: it is best to capture with the rook. This move attacks black's knight as well.

notes.text: Nc4 is your best move: it gets the knight out of the rook's way.
notes.original: Nc4 is the best move for black, getting out of the way of the rook. If you notice, Garry Kasparov's game with Boris Gelfand reached this position but in a different move order.

notes.text: Ng3 is White's most common move, making sure a knight lands on f5, at the cost of a pawn.
notes.original: Ng3 is the most common move for white, ensuring that a knight will land on f5. In exchange, white gives up a pawn.

notes.text: Take the free pawn.
notes.original: Black should take the free pawn.

notes.text: Ngf5 is the usual choice; White may feel better, but the position counts as equal.
notes.original: Ngf5 is more commonly played than Nhf5. Positionally white is probably better here but the position is considered to be equal.

notes.text: Your f-pawn attacks White's queen.
notes.original: The best move for black is to attack the queen with the f-pawn.

notes.text: White's queen retreats but stays on the g-file, keeping the knight on h4 supported.
notes.original: White's queen should retreat but stay on the g-file, preventing white's knight from getting booted.

notes.text: Your rook takes the c-file and can drop to c7 to support the g-pawn.
notes.original: Best move for black is to play Rc8. This is because Black takes control of the c-file (which we see in most Sicilians) and they can play Rc7 if need be which is reinforcing the g-pawn while being in front of the queen. Lastly, it provides protection for black's knight should white choose to attack it.

notes.text: Qb3 is the most common move: it attacks your loose knight.
notes.original: The most commonly played move is Qb3, attacking the loose knight.

notes.text: Your knight reaches safety on c4, where your rook on c8 now defends it.
notes.original: Black gets their knight to safety and on a decent square. Now we see the point of playing Rc8. The theory really ends here but I will show you a quick line that black must be weary of.

notes.text: White takes the d6 pawn and the material balance is restored.
notes.original: White can take the pawn on d6. Material balance has been restored.

notes.text: Recapture with the c-knight; it is the best way to take back.
notes.original: It is best to take with the c-knight.

notes.text: Taking back with your e-knight is impossible: White's rook move uncovers the queen's check on your king.
notes.original: You might be wondering why you can't take back the rook with your e-knight. This is because Rxd6 unleashes a discovered attack on the king.

notes.text: Your rook blocks the check. It is now pinned to your king, but this is still the best move.
notes.original: Though it is not always wise to pin your own pieces, this is the best move in the position.

notes.text: White's rook on d6 could be taken by your knight, so it has to retreat.
notes.original: White's rook should now retreat to safety because it can be taken now.

notes.text: Your g-pawn stops White's knight returning to f5 and gives your king a square on g7.
notes.original: Now it is best for black to play g6. This prevents white's knight from coming back to f5 and this creates an escape square for the king to unpin themselves.

notes.text: White simplifies with a3, and the right exchanges lead to a draw.
notes.original: The best move is to just play a3, simplifying the position and this will eventually lead to a draw with the right exchanges.

notes.text: Take on a3: White must find the only move, and if White takes your queen, you do better.
notes.original: I suggest taking the pawn on a3. This leads to forcing white to make an only move and to a trick if white takes your queen. Note that you can their queen too which will lead to an advantage.

notes.text: White should simply take the a-pawn back with the queen.
notes.original: So if you're playing white, please take the a-pawn.

notes.text: If White takes your queen, your a-pawn will likely promote and White's position collapses.
notes.original: If white takes your queen, you are winning because you will probably make a new queen with you a-pawn. White will be stuck defending against your promotion and their position will collapse. I'll show you the line with no explanation.

notes.text: Your rook offers a trade on d2 to simplify the position.
notes.original: From here I suggest playing Rd7 to just simplify the position.

notes.text: White should take your rook.
notes.original: White should take the rook.

notes.text: You recapture the rook with your queen.
notes.original: Black should recapture the rook.

notes.text: White can take the free pawn on a6.
notes.original: White can take the free pawn.

notes.text: Take the c-pawn and the position is equal; use the engine to practise converting to a draw.
notes.original: Black should capture white's c-pawn and now the position is completely equal with neither side having an advantage. That's as far as I'm going to go with this line. Trust me you do not need to know all of this theory, but if you want to outplay your opponent with theory and by knowing the ideas, then go ahead by all means. Feel free to use the engine to examine how to convert this to a draw :)

notes.text: White's position is collapsing here, and they can safely resign.
notes.original: As you can see, white's position is collapsing and they can safely resign.

notes.text: Develop normally: your knight comes out to c6 and hits the knight on d4.
notes.original: Black should develop normally.

notes.text: White is right to take your knight on c6.
notes.original: It's best for white to actually take this knight.

notes.text: Taking with the bishop is right, because White's knight fork is no longer a threat.
notes.original: Black can and should take with the bishop here because now there's no threat of a knight fork.

notes.text: With your bishop gone from d7, e6 lacks protection, so f5 works; White's light bishop is very strong.

notes.original: Now I will show you how to play the Kramnik Variation of the Sicilian Defense. This will be one of the only chapters that are in white's orientation only because this variation is really for white than it is for black. The Kramnik Sicilian is an attacking setup for white that was of course named after Vladimir Kramnik. You can use this variation to surprise opponents who typically play the e6 Sicilian. The variation is great because there are really only two variations you would ever have to know and white could hardly ever be worse in this opening. Now, the point of this move is to obviously prevent black from ever playing d5 and black can't really do anything about it. The only downside is that the light-squared bishop can only really be developed to e2.

notes.original: This is another variation of the Taimanov Variation. It's a much more aggressive variation in which white wants to plant their knight on d6. In order to stop this, black must play d6 themselves.

You can see the rest of the game here but it was truly a remarkable game from Kasparov and I believe this is a game that everyone should see just how positional value can change an entire game.
Karpov, Anatoly - Kasparov, Garry, 0-1, World Championship 32th-KK2, 1985, https://lichess.org/8ENETNzW

notes.text: Your knight on d6 is nicely placed, controlling the key central squares e4 and c4.
notes.original: Now black has a pretty nice knight on d6, controlling key central squares such as e4 and c4. I will stop the line here and we will evaluate the position. Black currently has tow weaknesses in the position. The first weakness is that c5 is currently loose and unguarded, but this can be resolved with a move like Nf5. The other weakness is that black's light-squared bishop still needs to be developed. As for white, there aren't obvious weaknesses other than the fact that the bishop on b3 isn't so optimally placed. I have shown black's plans in blue.

notes.text: Your c5 pawn is loose and your light bishop is undeveloped; a knight move like Nf5 is one answer.
notes.original: Now black has a pretty nice knight on d6, controlling key central squares such as e4 and c4. I will stop the line here and we will evaluate the position. Black currently has tow weaknesses in the position. The first weakness is that c5 is currently loose and unguarded, but this can be resolved with a move like Nf5. The other weakness is that black's light-squared bishop still needs to be developed. As for white, there aren't obvious weaknesses other than the fact that the bishop on b3 isn't so optimally placed. I have shown black's plans in blue.

notes.text: Your g6 is the most common reply: you prepare a fianchetto to fight for the dark squares.
notes.original: g6 is the most common response for black in which black prepares to fianchetto the bishop and fight on the dark squares as black knows that white will most likely put most of their pawns on light squares. Here there are two moves that white can play.

notes.text: White castles instead of taking on c6 right away; this is the most common choice.
notes.original: The most common response is to castle rather than taking the knight straight away.

notes.text: White may give up the bishop for your knight at once; this is also played often.
notes.original: White can choose to give up the bishop straight away rather than castling. This is also played very often. Black can take two ways here.

notes.text: Recapturing with the b-pawn is the more sensible choice positionally.
notes.original: Black of course can take with the b-pawn which makes a lot more sense positionally.

notes.text: Retaking with the d-pawn is by far the most common way and opens lines for your pieces.
notes.original: By far the most common way is to take with d-pawn, opening up black's pieces.

notes.text: White solidifies the pawn structure with d3.
notes.original: White should now solidify the pawn structure with d3.

notes.text: Your bishop reaches the long diagonal, as planned.
notes.original: Black will continue their plan of putting their bishop on the long-diagonal.

notes.text: White's h3 stops you from pinning the knight on f3 to the queen.
notes.original: White here should play h3, this prevents black from trying to pin white's knight to the queen. White wants to play this move because they need their knight to defend the dark-squares.

notes.text: You keep developing with your knight.
notes.original: Black continues their development.

notes.text: White develops too; you now have two main choices, and castling is the more popular.
notes.original: So does white. Here there are two moves here for black.

notes.text: Castling is the more popular choice for you here.
notes.original: Castling is more popular for black.

notes.text: White's bishop develops, guards the dark squares and attacks your c5 pawn.
notes.original: White should continue to develop and defend the dark-squares. This move also attacks the weak c-pawn.

notes.text: You must defend the c5 pawn, and b6 is the best way.
notes.original: Black has to defend and b6 is the best way to do that.

notes.text: White prepares Bh6 to trade off your g7 bishop, with the queen backing it up.
notes.original: Now white should play Qd2. White wants to play this so that they can get rid of black's bishop on g7.

notes.text: Your e5 gains central control, and White shouldn't capture it.
notes.original: Now e5 should be played by black, gaining some control in the center. White really shouldn't take this pawn on e5,

notes.text: White's bishop goes after your powerful g7 bishop to trade it off.
notes.original: Now white should get rid of black's powerful bishop.

notes.text: Taking e5 is a mistake: you reply Nxe4 and win the piece back with your bishop.
notes.original: This is because black can play a tactical move here and play Nxe4. I'll show you the line briefly.

notes.text: Let White take your bishop; your queen is central on d6 and defends the e5 pawn.
notes.original: Black should allow the bishop to be taken and centralize their queen and defending the e-pawn..

notes.text: White takes your bishop on g7, and you will retake with the king.
notes.original: White should now capture the bishop.

notes.text: Retaking with your king is the only move here.
notes.original: Only move for black.

notes.text: White castles kingside and plans to play on the queenside.
notes.original: Now white should castle king-side and prepare to play on the queen-side.

notes.text: Your rook centralizes on e8 and protects the e5 pawn.
notes.original: Black will now play Re8 and centralize their rook, protecting the e-pawn.

notes.text: White's a4 pawn puts a brake on your b-pawn by controlling b5.
notes.original: Now white plays the crucial move, a4. This is a move that white will usually play when white trades off the bishop for the knight on c6 and when black captures with the d-pawn. This can be applied to most positions like this in chess. This is because you want to put a brake on black's move, b5.

notes.text: You will usually answer White's a4 with a5.
notes.original: Black will usually respond with a5.

notes.text: White's b3 supports the a4 pawn and builds a light-square pawn triangle.
notes.original: Then white will play b3, solidifying a4 and creating a nice pawn triangle on the light squares because the light-squared bishop has been traded off. I will stop the line here but feel free to examine how to play this position further.

notes.text: You are still left with your powerful bishop, now on e5.
notes.original: Black is still left with their powerful bishop.

notes.text: Nc6 is your main move and holds back White's d4 push.
notes.original: Nc6 is the main move for black and is really the only trying move that black has which is somewhat preventing the d4 push. Here is where the position branches out.

notes.text: Nc3 is White's most common reply, a quiet setup familiar from the English Opening.
notes.original: White's most common response is Nc3 which is very commonly seen in the English Opening setups. This is the more passive approach to this position. Here black has two choices.

notes.text: White's d4 is the more aggressive approach; Kramnik beat Kasparov with this variation.
notes.original: White can still play d4 however which is the more aggressive approach to this position. Vladimir Kramnik actually beat Garry Kasparov thru this aggressive variation and you can go check that game out.

notes.text: Developing the knight to f6 is your most common approach.
notes.original: Black can develop normally and play Nf6 which is the most common approach.

notes.text: White develops and prepares to castle; you could still close the centre with e5, but it is rarer.
notes.original: White will continue to develop normally and prepare to castle. Note that black can still play e5 to close down the position if they want but that is not the most common move.

notes.text: Strike in the centre with d5 to disrupt White's bind on that square.
notes.original: Black should strike in the center now with d5. This move seems rather impossible but all black is doing is that they're trying to disrupt the bind that white has on d5.

notes.text: White takes on d5 with the e-pawn.
notes.original: White should take with the e-pawn here.

notes.text: Recapture the pawn on d5 with your e-pawn.
notes.original: Black should recapture the pawn.

notes.text: White plays d4 instead of retaking, and the game branches out again.
notes.original: Instead of taking back the pawn once again, instead white can play that crucial d4 push now. We can see why the e5 push for black is important in some positions because now this move is possible for white. From here, black has many choices and the game branches out again.

notes.text: Be6 is your most common move, reinforcing the d5 pawn.
notes.original: The most common move is Be6, reinforcing the d5 pawn.

notes.text: White takes the d5 pawn anyway.
notes.original: White should go ahead and take this pawn anyway.

notes.text: Retake with the knight, not the bishop; there is no reason to give up your bishop.
notes.original: Black should take with the knight here as there's absolutely no reason for black to give up the bishop pair here.

notes.text: White castles here; only two replies have ever been played for Black.
notes.original: Now white should castle. Here only two moves have ever been played for black.

notes.text: Be7 is the most common move; it prepares castling, and a series of exchanges follows.
notes.original: The most common move is to play Be7, preparing to castle. Now a series of exchanges are about to occur.

notes.text: White takes your c5 pawn with its d-pawn, starting the exchanges.
notes.original: White should take the pawn on c5 now.

notes.text: You capture White's knight on c3.
notes.original: Black should capture white's knight.

notes.text: White recaptures the knight with the b-pawn. Your next two options are equally popular.
notes.original: White should recapture the knight. Here two moves have been played an equal amount of times.

notes.text: The engine slightly prefers Bxc5: keep the tension and don't hand White the open d-file.
notes.original: The engine favors Bxc5 more ever so slightly and it makes sense considering that it's very common in chess to keep the tension and to not want to give white the open d-file when the rook recaptures.

notes.text: White's knight attacks your bishop on e6 and threatens to take it, ending your bishop pair.
notes.original: Now Ng5 should be played, threatening to take black's bishop pair and to capture the pawn on g7.

notes.text: You must trade queens: your queen takes White's on d1.
notes.original: Now black must trade queens.

notes.text: White recaptures with the rook to take control of the d-file.
notes.original: White should recapture with the rook to gain control of the d-file.

notes.text: You castle here to get your king to safety.
notes.original: Black should castle here.

notes.text: White puts its dark-squared bishop on f4, where it has the most scope; White has largely achieved its goals.
notes.original:
Now white should develop the dark-squared bishop to where it has the most scope. From here the game branches out once more. You don't really need to know that much theory here as white has pretty much achieved everything that they wanted. I will highlight the strengths and weaknesses on both sides and the plans for white.

notes.text: You centralize your f-rook on the e-file.
notes.original: I will go ahead and show some more theory if you are curious. From here black centralizes the f-rook.

notes.text: White's king steps to f1: closer to the pieces for the endgame, and safe from back-rank mates.
notes.original: Kf1 is the engine's top choice and is tied for the most commonly played move. In positions where the queens are the off-board, it is common for both sides to have their kings not too far away from their pieces so that they may be active in an endgame. This also stop any back-rank checkmates.

notes.text: You centralize your other rook and offer a rook trade, but engines say White is better.
notes.original: The most common move for black is to centralize the other rook and is offering a rook trade. According to the engines, white now has an advantage here.

notes.text: White's knight takes your bishop on e6, getting rid of your bishop pair.
notes.original: White should get rid of black's bishop pair.

notes.text: You will most likely exchange rooks, here with check on d1.
notes.original: Black will most likely exchange rooks now.

notes.text: White recaptures on d1 with the rook.
notes.original: White should definitely recapture with the rook.

notes.text: Taking with the rook is probably best, since it keeps your kingside pawns connected.
notes.original: It is probably best to capture with the rook here and to keep black's king-side pawns connected.

notes.text: White's rook attacks your bishop on c5 and will capture it unless you move it.
notes.original: Rd5 is white's best move and is tied for the most commonly played move. The threat is to obviously capture the bishop. Now we can see the importance of Kf1 may I add.

notes.text: Bb6 is best and theory ends here; it avoids weakening yourself with b6. White is slightly better.
notes.original: Bb6 is the best move here and this is where the theory ends as this is considered to be a novelty. This is the best move because black doesn't want to create any sort of weaknesses for themselves with the move b6. I will stop the review of this line here but feel free to evaluate this position further. White is slightly better in this position according to the engines.
